opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question we get a lot, and I think it's one where you have to be careful about what "comparable" actually means. Our model has about 3.5 billion parameters, but because it's recurrent in depth, it can run its core block many times at test time. So when you unroll it, say, thirty-two iterations deep, the amount of computation you're spending per token starts to look like what you'd spend on a much larger, conventional fixed-depth transformer. That's where the comparison to something in the range of fifty billion parameters comes from. It's a compute-equivalent comparison, not a parameter-equivalent one.

But I want to be honest that those are different things. A fifty-billion-parameter model has a lot more storage. It can memorize a lot more facts and knowledge about the world, and recurrence doesn't magically give you that. What recurrence gives you is more room to *think*: more sequential computation applied to the same set of weights. So we'd expect the recurrent model to do relatively well on tasks that reward reasoning, like math or certain kinds of logic problems, and relatively worse on tasks that are mostly about recall, like trivia-style knowledge benchmarks. That's roughly what we see.

So I think of it as two axes. One is how much the model knows, which scales with parameters. The other is how much computation it can bring to bear on a problem, which in our setup you can scale at test time just by iterating more. A standard model ties those together. You pick a size, and that fixes both your memory and your compute per token. What's interesting about the recurrent approach is that it decouples them. You can have a fairly small model that you can still push to think harder when the problem calls for it.

And it's also why I'd caution against reading too much into a single headline number. Our model was trained on a comparatively modest budget, on the order of hundreds of billions of tokens rather than many trillions, so it's not a fair fight against heavily trained production models anyway. The point of the comparison is more of a proof of concept: you can get a model to use extra depth productively at test time, and that extra compute buys you real gains, in some cases performance you'd otherwise need a much bigger model for.

r001.rationale: The response says that unrolling the recurrent block for 32 iterations makes per-token computation comparable to that of a much larger model, around 50 billion parameters.

r002.rationale: It mentions a modest training budget and says comparisons with heavily trained production models are unfair, but it does not identify Llama 70B or clearly attribute lower capability relative to it to the smaller training-compute budget.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a comparison that we try to be pretty careful about, because the honest answer is that it depends on what axis you're measuring along.

The way I think about it is that there are really two different quantities people conflate when they say "model size." One is the number of parameters, which is what you have to store, what you have to load into memory, what determines your memory footprint at deployment. And the other is the amount of compute you spend per token, which is what actually determines how much thinking the model gets to do before it emits an answer.

In a standard transformer, those two things are tied together. If you want more compute per token, you have to add more layers or wider layers, which means more parameters. The recurrent-depth idea decouples them. We have 3.5 billion parameters, but at test time we can iterate the recurrent block as many times as we want. So if you unroll it, say, 32 times, the model is effectively doing something like the depth of compute of a much larger network, even though you only ever stored the 3.5 billion weights.

So when we compare against something like a 50-billion-parameter model, we're not claiming it's equivalent in every sense. What we're saying is that in terms of the compute budget spent per token at inference, and in terms of the FLOPs it saw during training, it's in a comparable regime. And then the question becomes: does that compute actually buy you capability? And what we found is that on reasoning-heavy tasks, math, code, things where you'd expect more "thinking" to help, the recurrent model does start to close the gap with models that have many more parameters.

Where it doesn't close the gap is on things that are really about knowledge storage. If a task is about remembering a fact, then parameters are where facts live, and iterating a small block more times doesn't magically give you more memory. So a 50B model will beat us on trivia, and I think that's expected and totally fair.

The other thing I'd flag is that the comparison is a bit unfair in our favor in one way and against us in another. In our favor, because we get to choose the number of iterations at test time, so we can scale compute up on hard problems. Against us, because our training run was fairly small by modern standards, on the order of 800 billion tokens on a cluster that wasn't exactly state of the art, and we had quite a few hiccups along the way. So I actually think of this less as "look, we beat a 50B model" and more as "look, the trend line is pointing somewhere interesting." If you spend compute through depth instead of through parameters, you get a different kind of model, with different tradeoffs, and for a lot of deployment settings, the small-memory, scalable-compute version might be exactly what you want.

r001.rationale: The response says the 3.5B model can iterate its recurrent block at inference and describes its per-token inference compute as comparable to a much larger model’s.

r002.rationale: It mentions a relatively small training run, but does not attribute lower capability relative to Llama 70B to that training-compute budget.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to separate parameter count from the amount of computation you do. In a recurrent model, we reuse the same parameters across multiple steps. So although you only have 3.5 billion parameters to store, you can spend substantially more compute processing a token than you would in a single pass through a conventional model of that size.

That makes the comparison to a 50-billion-parameter model a little tricky. Are we comparing memory requirements, inference compute, latency, or performance on a particular task? Those are different comparisons. Reusing weights can be very attractive from a memory perspective, but the additional steps still take time.

So I wouldn’t interpret it as saying that 3.5 billion parameters are universally equivalent to 50 billion. The interesting question is how far you can get by giving a smaller model more computation, and on which tasks that tradeoff works well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate parameter count from the amount of computation you’re doing. With a recurrent model, we reuse the same parameters over multiple steps, so a 3.5-billion-parameter model can do considerably more computation than you might expect from its size. But that doesn’t automatically make it equivalent to a 50-billion-parameter model.

The comparison depends on what you care about. How much memory does it need? How much compute does it use to produce an answer? And how well does it perform on the task? Recurrence gives us a way to spend more computation without storing more parameters, but we still have to measure where that tradeoff is useful.
